transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-11-12 16:00 PST | Duration: ~55m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Emily Park (Shoreline Head of ML), Rohit Singh (SRE), Lena Ortiz (PM)

Summary: quick POC scoping focused on workload characterization and traffic modeling for Shoreline Bank's conversational assistant pilot. Goal is to agree success criteria, sizing (QPS / concurrency), benchmark plan and timeline.

Topics: success criteria, QPS & concurrency estimates, input/output token distribution, latency & cost targets, dedicated vs hosted, security requirements, next steps and owners.

00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intros.
00:18 Emily: hi, emily here, we run the ML team, leading the banking assistant POC, thanks for fitting us in.
00:30 Maya: great, i'll give a quick overview of what Redwood will provide then we dig into traffic. Carlos will drive the workload modeling.
00:50 Carlos: hey, hi, yeah so goal is to size the POC to reflect peak production-ish traffic and make sure our benchmarks line up.
01:15 Lena: just to set context, our product expects to serve 1st release to 50k customers, internal estimate of 3k DAUs, peak trade hours around noon-to-2pm.
01:40 Rohit: infra note — we need the solution to live in a VPC for data-flow, and we will push for KMS integration if we go dedicated or private.
02:05 Carlos: noted. can we start with current latency and architecture? emily, what are you running today?
02:22 Emily: currently prototype uses in-house GPU infra with an open LLM (we call it "shoreline-ops"), avg p95 latency about 600-800ms for 200 tokens outputs, but costs are high and stability is meh.
02:45 Maya: ok, so target improvements are cost stability and lower p95. what does success look like for you?
03:00 Emily: success criteria — p95 latency under 300ms for typical queries, end-to-end transaction time under 500ms for synchronous flows, quality parity with current model (no notable regressions on our core prompts), and a weekly cost under our cap (TBD $).
03:26 Carlos: we'll capture that. on modeling side we need QPS and concurrency numbers. emily, any telemetry on request distribution?
03:40 Emily: rough current numbers: avg QPS ~80 globally during core business hours, spike QPS up to 380 for batch events, average input prompt length 90-150 tokens, average output 180-260 tokens. about 60% of calls are short status checks (~40 tokens out), 25% are form-fills (~300 tokens), 15% long explanations.
04:20 Maya: interesting, so for POC let's try to emulate peak ridership — i'd propose we model for a steady 120 QPS with 10-20 concurrency and bursts to 400 QPS for 30s. does that map to what you see?
04:45 Emily: yes that's reasonable; our ops want the burst tolerance.
05:00 Carlos: quick note on concurrency: concurrency here we mean number of simultaneous open model sessions, which depends on generation length and response time. with 220 avg output tokens and 0.6 tokens/ms on a given GPU, concurrency will be higher. so we model both QPS and average response token latency.
05:30 Rohit: can you translate that into GPUs or pods? we need a sizing estimate for our sandbox.
05:44 Carlos: rough estimate for open 13B-like model: with Redwood's runtime, continuous batching, and quantized model we can serve ~60-80 effective QPS per GPU at 4-8 token/ms generation depending on config — which is a little fuzzy but for POC we propose provisioning capacity to cover peak burst with autoscaling. for deterministic numbers: to handle 120 steady QPS + headroom, plan for 2 GPUs; to handle 400 burst for 30s with acceptable tail latency you'd want 6-8 GPUs or rely on Redwood's burst policy to fall back to slightly higher-latency instances.
06:30 Maya: also decision point: hosted vs dedicated for POC. hosted gives faster start; dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable latency and isolation. thoughts?
06:52 Emily: for POC we prefer dedicated sandbox in our VPC if possible, mainly for KMS and audit logs. but if timeline is tight we could start hosted while we prep security.
07:10 Lena: timeline sensitivity — product wants demo to execs by first week of dec, so POC needs to run benchmarks and provide report by 2027-11-29.
07:30 Maya: ok that's tight but doable. benchmark run ideally next week 11/22-11/24.
07:45 Carlos: benchmark plan: two phases — functional correctness and quality checks using your prompt set (sample of 200 prompts), then performance benchmarking with simulated traffic at multiple profiles: steady 120 QPS, 400 QPS burst, and a long-tail test with 25% long outputs. we'll measure p50/p95/p99 latency, token/sec, GPU util, and cost per 1k responses.
08:15 Emily: also please include cold-start and KV cache warmup — our flows sometimes rely on a prefix context that's cacheable.
08:30 Carlos: yes we'll instrument KV cache hit rates and prefix caching impact. small note — transcription might say K V cache in the notes, but we mean KV cache.
08:45 Rohit: security — SOC2, SAML SSO, KMS support, audit logs, data retention policies. can you share baseline docs?
09:00 Maya: yes, we'll attach SOC2, SSO guide, and KMS integration docs. for private/VPC we can set up a private control plane or air-gapped if required but that's later.
09:18 Emily: success metrics recap: p95 <300ms typical; quality parity on 200 prompt set (no more than 2% regression on top-1 intent accuracy); cost target TBD but estimate per-call cost target should be less than current.
09:40 Carlos: for traffic modeling i'll propose a distribution: 60% short (<=50 input tokens, 40-80 output tokens), 25% medium (50-200 input, 150-300 output), 15% long (>200 input, 300-800 output). average input ~120 tokens, average output ~220 tokens.
10:10 Maya: that aligns with what you said earlier. we'll use those buckets in the benchmark runner.
10:22 Lena: how about concurrency math? show us quick calc so ops can size.
10:30 Carlos: sure — concurrency ~= QPS * avg_response_time. avg_response_time depends on output tokens and tokens/sec. assume generation at 50 tokens/sec effective (varies by model/hardware); with 220 tokens that's ~4.4s generation plus decoding/overheads => ~5s response. 120 QPS * 5s => 600 concurrent model requests if naive, but batching and streaming reduce effective load. Redwood's runtime converts many of those to pipelined workloads so observed GPU-level concurrency is lower. for pod sizing we measure effective QPS per GPU — our historical numbers for similar workloads: 40-90 effective QPS per GPU depending on batching and quantization.
11:20 Rohit: that 600 number sounds scary — can you explain the batching effect?
11:30 Carlos: yes so a lot of those 5s windows are overlapping token generation which the runtime batches across requests. continuous batching and KV cache make average GPU compute more efficient. rather than 600 separate small kernels we do aggregated kernels, so GPU utilization goes up and per-request cost goes down. in practice we've seen the padded-token overhead dominate for highly variable lengths, so we'll test with your real prompt distribution.
12:05 Emily: for the benchmark please include our high-cost prompts (legal/regulatory QA) because they generate long outputs and are business-critical.
12:20 Maya: noted. also we'll measure A/B quality vs your current model and produce a baseline report.
12:40 Carlos: regarding fallback policies — if capacity is constrained we can route to smaller model variants (quantized or distilled) with explicit quality degradation metrics, or spill to queued async flows for non-urgent ops. do you have rules about synchronous vs async?
13:10 Lena: synchronous for customer-facing flows (chat/transactions), async okay for batch reporting.
13:25 Maya: tech ops question — Rohit, will you be able to provide a test VPC or do you prefer Redwood deploy a private node?
13:35 Rohit: we'll provision a sandbox VPC and provide temporary creds, KMS integration may require our security team sign-off.
13:48 Carlos: for SLOs during POC we recommend p95 < 400ms for steady and p95 < 700ms during burst for the first run, with final target 300ms after tuning.
14:10 Emily: ok that's fair as an initial SLO to validate.
14:20 Maya: cost modeling — Carlos, can you give a ballpark cost per 1k responses for the proposed config?
14:30 Carlos: ballpark for a quantized 13B on dedicated GPUs with batching: $X to $Y per 1k responses. (note: we gave an initial estimate in the call — exact numbers in the SOW). for planning use $0.80-1.50 per 1k responses as a placeholder depending on model and quantization.
15:00 Lena: ops need numbers in $ to decide procurement, please make that explicit in the SOW.
15:10 Maya: will do.
15:22 Carlos: benchmarks we'll capture: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU util, KV cache hit rate, batching efficiency, cost-per-token and cost-per-1k-responses. we'll run at 3 profiles: baseline 60 QPS, prod-like 120 QPS steady, and burst 400 QPS for 30-60s with warm and cold cache tests.
15:58 Emily: timeline recap? we need results and report by 11/29.
16:05 Maya: deliverables: benchmark report + quality A/B + SOW with pricing + security docs. owners and dates in action items.
16:20 Rohit: one more note on compliance — we will need audit logs exported to our SIEM; is log export supported?
16:30 Maya: yes — audit logs and per-route tracing available, we'll include config steps.
16:42 Carlos: small transcription artifact — sometimes product names show as RedWood Deicated in notes; we use Redwood Dedicated for reserved capacity.
16:55 Lena: ok, last question: do you support model pinning and rollbacks?
17:05 Maya: yes — rollouts, canary deploys, and automatic fallback policies are supported. we can pin model versions per-route.
17:20 Emily: great. any more questions?
17:30 Maya: nope, thanks everyone. quick recap of next steps then we'll wrap.
17:45 (wrap)

Notes on modeling numbers captured during call:
- Recommended POC traffic profiles: steady 120 QPS, burst 400 QPS for 30s, baseline 60 QPS for long-tail tests.
- Token distribution buckets: short 60%, medium 25%, long 15%; avg input 120 tokens, avg output 220 tokens.
- Concurrency approximation: naive concurrency = QPS * avg_resp_time; using 5s avg resp => 120*5 = 600 concurrent in-flight requests (logical), but GPU-level effective concurrency much lower due to batching.
- GPU sizing heuristic: expect 40-90 effective QPS per GPU for quantized 13B; for steady 120 QPS plan for 2 GPUs with autoscale; for burst to 400 consider 6-8 GPUs or fallback policy.
- Success criteria: p95 < 300ms (final), initial POC SLO p95 < 400ms steady, p95 <700ms during burst; quality parity on 200-prompt eval set with <2% regression.
- Security/compliance: SOC2, KMS integration, SAML SSO, audit logs to SIEM required; Redwood to provide docs.

Links / artifacts referenced: benchmark spec (will be shared by Carlos), sample prompt set (Shoreline to provide), SOC2 and KMS docs (Maya to attach), draft SOW/pricing (Maya).

Action items (flattened):
- Maya Chen: Send draft SOW and pricing by 2027-11-15.
- Carlos Ruiz: Share benchmark spec, runner scripts, and sample payloads by 2027-11-14.
- Emily Park: Confirm dataset access and compliance contacts by 2027-11-18.
